20477-the-book-of-ballads-edited-by-bon-:
The Book of Ballads edited by Bon Gaultier collects the comic and romantic ballads written for Blackwood's Magazine. Bon Gaultier was the shared pen name behind the pieces. The editor's memoir tells how he and William Edmonstoune Aytoun came together in the work.

Aytoun was born on June 21, 1813, three years before his partner. He was already known as a writer in Blackwood's when the two joined forces. For two or three years they wrote together in literature. Their ballads parodied famous poems and mocked public figures, and readers of the magazine prized their polish and bite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adolphe-perra:
Adolphe Perraud was a cardinal and academician born at Lyons on 7 February 1828, who died on 18 February 1906. He shone at the lycees Henri IV and St. Louis, entered the Ecole Normale under Gratry's influence, won the history fellowship in 1850, and taught two years at Angers. In 1852 he left teaching for the priesthood and joined the Oratory in Paris, then being reorganized by Gratry and Petetot.

Ordained in 1855 after a stay at Rome, he became history professor and religion prefect at St. Lo's petit seminaire, while devoting himself to preaching. In 1860 he visited Ireland and wrote Contemporary Ireland in 1862. In 1866 the Sorbonne made him its ecclesiastical history professor, treating Protestantism brilliantly. Made Bishop of Autun in 1874 despite liberal tendencies, he served working men closely, preaching the funeral sermon after the Montceau mining disaster killed twenty-two.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-domin:
Antoine-Dominique Magaud, a French painter born at Marseilles in 1817, led the city's art school so well that he was called its second founder. Trained in Paris under Léon Cogniet, he painted portraits and landscapes, yet his real strength lay in large decorative work. Across Marseilles he adorned the Chamber of Commerce, the library, the prefecture, and grand hotels.

His masterpiece was a historical gallery for the Marseilles Religious Association, with fifteen great canvases and a vast ceiling. Its theme glorified Christian civilization, with religion shown as the source that inspires learning, science, and art. Side walls carried scenes from philosophy to the early martyrs, and the entry ranks Magaud among the finest decorative painters of his city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustus-theb:
Augustus Thebaud was a Jesuit educator and publicist born at Nantes in France in 1807, who died at Fordham in New York in 1885. His parents, a merchant and his pious wife, married during the Terror by a loyal priest, and their children received France's best religious schooling then. Thebaud studied at Nantes, was ordained, and worked three years in parishes before entering the Society of Jesus in Italy in 1835. He then studied science at the Sorbonne under Ampere.

He reached the United States in December 1838. He took the chemistry chair at St Mary's College in Kentucky, becoming its rector in 1846. That year the Jesuits moved to St John's College, Fordham, where Thebaud served as first Jesuit president from 1846 to 1851 and again from 1860 to 1863. Between and after those terms he pastored St Joseph's at Troy. From 1875 until his death he wrote his reminiscences in three volumes, energetic even in old age.

govdocs-archive_org-propaganda-the-forma:
Jacques Ellul, the French sociologist, published Propaganda: The Formation of Men's Attitudes in French in 1962, and it reached English readers in 1965. Ellul argues that propaganda is not a few posters or speeches. It is a whole condition of modern life.

Governments, parties, advertisers, and media together shape what whole societies think, often without any single liar in charge. Ellul insists that educated people are propaganda's best targets, not its safeguards. The book became a classic of media theory, and its cold view of mass persuasion still unsettles readers who meet it today.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cybervault_HR_494:
H. R. 4943 carries a long name, the Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act, shortened to the CLOUD Act. A National Security Archive cyber brief explains what the act does. It lets American law enforcement serve warrants and subpoenas for data stored on servers anywhere in the world. The one condition is that the company holding the data is based in the United States.

That rule settled a fight that had reached the Supreme Court, over whether a warrant could reach email stored in another country. Where data physically sits no longer controls the answer; who holds it does. For readers, the brief is a plain-language guide to a law that quietly reshaped privacy and policing across borders. It remains a reference point in every later argument over government access to cloud data.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-the-co:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of the Court of St. Cloud selects from an account credited to a gentleman at Paris, covering Napoleon's court at Saint-Cloud. David Widger's extracts run alphabetically, sentence by sentence, through the manners and fears of the new empire.

Bonaparte and his wife go every morning to hear Mass, one entry reports, yet Bonaparte dreads the liberty of the press more than all else. Priests are to be proscribed as criminals, creditors are denounced and executed, and a figure called the Chevalier of the Guillotine appears. Power forcing the law is the refrain of the whole bitter selection.
the-lady-of-the-shroud:
Bram Stoker, author of Dracula, published this novel with Rider and Company of London in 1909, dedicating it to his old friend the Comtesse de Guerbel, the actress Genevieve Ward. It opens not with a narrator but with a clipping from The Journal of Occultism, mid-January 1907, reporting a strange story from the Adriatic. On the night of the ninth, the steamship Victorine passed the Spear of Ivan on the coast of the Blue Mountains a little before midnight.

The lookout called the captain to a tiny floating light close inshore, where ships had once hugged the coast so closely that Lloyd's had warned of the risk. Captain Mirolani slowed the engines and edged in to investigate possible distress, joined by his officers and by a passenger, Mr. Peter Caulfield, known for reports of spiritual phenomena. Stoker frames his shrouded lady as a documented mystery, attested by signatures.
